narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Being in the second decile is substantially lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling weaker long-term academic performance in law school.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 39, it sits above the average of 37.2 among accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the third most important feature. It is slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and therefore nudged the outcome modestly toward failure.

Taken together, the model concluded that your lower third-year class standing outweighed the positive signal from your LSAT, resulting in an overall risk of failure that crossed the rejection threshold.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake courses or seek additional academic support to raise your class rank, consider retaking the LSAT to push that score even higher, and then reapply. Many students improve these exact factors and gain admission on a second attempt.
